conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospitalists. You're here today for your scheduled IVIG infusion, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I come in every two weeks for this. It helps with my immune system, but it can be rough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve been on a half-dose regimen now for a few months. Can you tell me what kind of side effects you usually get?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Usually, about 12 hours after, I get chest tightness, shortness of breath, and feel like I’m going to heave the next morning. It’s delayed, not right during the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll monitor you closely. You also mentioned something about an episode at home yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes — power went out, no heat. I felt the cold get to me. My heart started skipping, then slowed down. I almost passed out, but it only lasted about 15 seconds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. But you recovered on your own, no chest pain or lasting symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it passed quickly. But I’ve had heart issues before — stents, SVT. And with my mitochondrial disease, my autonomic system doesn’t regulate well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. That makes you more sensitive to temperature and stress. We’ll keep you on telemetry to watch your heart rhythm during the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. I also get tingling in my hands sometimes during the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll slow the rate if that happens. Tingling can be a mild reaction to IVIG. We’ll premedicate you with Benadryl and Tylenol to help prevent reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And I’ve already had two liters of saline overnight — helps with the orthostatic hypotension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your usual IV fluids. Your vitals now are stable — BP 130 over 86, pulse 76, oxygen 98% on room air. You’re looking good so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m glad I’m not having fever or chills this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection today. Labs from this morning are normal — white count, kidney function, electrolytes all stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My main concern is getting through the infusion without too much trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re set up for that. We’ll start the IVIG in about 30 minutes after your premeds. We’ll go slow and watch you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve taken your Benadryl and Tylenol. We’re starting the Gammagard infusion now at a low rate — 15 grams total.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I feel it starting. Nothing unusual yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling now? It’s been about 45 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m starting to feel a little short of breath. And my chest feels tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen level is 96%, so you’re not hypoxic. I’ll put you on 2 liters of oxygen through a nasal cannula to help you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That already helps. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also slow the infusion rate. Let’s see if that reduces your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also noticing a tingling in my fingers again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common and often improves when we slow the rate. We’re doing that now. Any numbness in your face or lips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. No signs of a serious allergic reaction. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re halfway through, and your symptoms seem to be improving. Oxygen is helping, and the tingling has lessened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel more comfortable now. The chest tightness is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news — the infusion is complete. You tolerated it well, all things considered. We’ll keep you on oxygen for a bit longer and monitor you overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it’s over. I’ll probably feel tired tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Rest up. We’ll check on you through the night. Your heart rhythm has been stable on telemetry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No chest tightness, no shortness of breath. I did feel a little queasy this morning, but it passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common — part of your delayed reaction. But since you’re otherwise feeling well, and your vitals are stable, we can plan for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. No changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. You stayed on your home medications — aspirin, Plavix, metoprolol, atorvastatin, valsartan, Nexium, and the others. We just monitored you during the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep getting IV fluids three times a week at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. And your next IVIG is in two weeks. We recommend continuing hospital admission for those infusions given your reaction history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I feel safer here during the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send discharge instructions to your primary team. Follow up with Dr. ___ for your immunodeficiency and cardiology as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have the nurse finalize discharge paperwork. You should be out by mid-morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you’re still feeling well this morning? No new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, still feeling back to normal. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Your discharge exam shows stable vitals — pulse 56, BP 142 over 80, oxygen 97% on room air. Lungs clear, heart regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. I’ll keep an eye on how I feel over the next day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or pass out, go to the ER. Otherwise, keep to your routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll be careful with temperature changes — that cold episode scared me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Stay warm, hydrated, and listen to your body. We’ll see you next infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. You’re cleared for discharge.
